group.passage:
A mother, her face streaked with tears, sobbed uncontrollably as William H. Mumler, the spirit photographer, revealed the photo. In it, she stared blankly at the camera, while a ghostly, indistinct figure—strikingly similar to her deceased daughter—rested its tiny hand on her lap. It’s easy to see why 19th-century Americans fell under Mumler’s spell. The Civil War had left countless families [[1]], and in a nation reeling from loss, the idea of capturing a glimpse of a dead loved one offered a sliver of hope. Mumler was later charged with fraud, yet how he managed to [[2]] remains a mystery more than 150 years later.
His career as a spirit photographer began by accident. An amateur [[3]], Mumler was practicing self-portraits when one of his prints came back with an unexplainable aberration. Though he had been alone in the room, the image showed what appeared to be the ghostly figure of his cousin—dead for 12 years. A businessman at heart, Mumler seized the opportunity, promoting his haunted photograph to the mainstream press. The [[4]] brought him swift fortune, convincing him to pursue photography as a lifelong profession.
Unsurprisingly, his spirit photographs attracted skeptics, [[5]] sought to expose his dirty deeds—among them the famous J.W. Black. The experienced photographer sat for a portrait in Mumler’s studio, closely observing the entire process, and yet found nothing suspicious. Though Mumler was eventually tried for fraud in 1869, he pleaded not guilty and continued working in photography afterward.
